brief_extract: Price 3/-. Three major issues ring in the mind after reading “Posture in Housework”: that good carriage is a basis of good health, increases mental alertness, and, to quote Professor Winifred Cullis’ foreword, “enables work to be done more efficiently and with less fatigue.” These generalities are substantiated by tests carried out by Miss Maughan, the Principal, and the Staff of the National Society’s College, and show the possibilities for improvements in most methods of doing commonplace household tasks, if some thought be given to posture. Custom of course dies hard, and it is unlikely that those who have habitual ways will change to new methods; indeed, in many instances custom, developed from instinct and experience, has by science been proved right; but Miss Maughan in this presentation of the principles of posture gives cause for thought.

of the domestic worker. It is resolved therefore
that facilities for gaining a greater knowledge and
understanding of this new service should be avail-
able to everyone engaged in household duties, that
this great benefit of the modern electrical age shall
be shared by all."

By Service of Electricity
THE Dowager Lady Swaythling, Vice-President
of the E.A.W., when introducing the Resolu-
tion, explained that it is the purpose of the
Association to organise classes of instruction to give
rudimentary knowledge of domestic electrical
housecraft and appliances. In this way domestic
workers will have every opportunity of learning to
what a great extent science can help them in their
tasks, and how to get the maximum efficiency from
the equipment at their disposal.

By JOYCE WEDGWOOD

FOURTEEN years ago we in this country found our-selves on the threshold of a new age — the age of broadcasting. No one in 1922 ever visualised what a complete revolution the coming of the radio receiving set into our homes was to make in the social life of the community, how every important national event would be brought to our firesides, and we would be enabled by this modern miracle to be present at all the major happenings of the world, to rejoice in company with the whole Empire, or even to await in solemnity the passing of a King.
